subtitle: Trade Recap - Here's What I've Been Buying and Selling
title: September 2026 Portfolio Review
description: Trade Recap - Here's What I've Been Buying and Selling
body_html:
Disclaimer: By reading this article, you acknowledge and agree to the terms and conditions

It’s been almost three months since the last Portfolio Review on June 12th, but it feels like a lifetime has passed by and that things are crazier than ever, doesn’t it?

The craziness isn’t merely anecdotal, it’s evident in the indices: S&P 500 sectors continue to trade like warring factions rather than correlated, friendly peers.

Some of the correlations are a result of “sensible” connections, for example rising Crude Oil prices helping the Energy Sector at the expense of everyone else. Still, with historical correlations between the Consumer Staples, Consumer Discretionary, Semiconductors, Banks, and Financial Sectors to the S&P coming in below the 10th percentile, it’s evident that a lot is going on beneath the surface of a relatively calm S&P 500 performance, especially as crowded AI exposure across pod shops and trading desks amplifies these swings through repeated cycles of grossing up and panic-induced selling.

Take, for example, the 15% surge in Regional Banks and Insurance during the late-June to mid-August “flight to safety” as the Memory Sector and Nvidia imploded 15-30%. Did the liquidation of the AI trade lead to a change in fundamentals that made Regional Banks and Insurers justifiably worth 15% more? Of course not, and the knee-jerk move up provided an excellent opportunity to exit overvalued financials names before the trend quickly reversed in September (as we’ll discuss further in the Portfolio Review).

As ironic as this sounds, I think the craziness is coming from a logical place. Countless traders and investors have reasonably concluded the World is changing at an ever-increasing pace, and this has prompted them to believe there’s only limited time to “escape the permanent underclass” and take outsized risk to do so. I don’t believe this is the right thing to do, but the graphs below illustrate where they are coming from.

Source: OpenRouter

Source: BLS Data (Courtesy of ChatGPT)

Token usage continues to inflect higher. OpenRouter is a platform that gives developers access to hundreds of leading models via a unified API (Application Programming Interface). Their reports regularly reflect 15-20% increases in weekly token usage, which I believe shows just how fast things are accelerating. This isn’t a monthly or quarterly figure, it’s weekly. AI is getting larger, and it’s getting larger quickly.

On the other hand, US employment reports continue to paint a gloomy picture. While the bond market and US Equity Investors gleefully cheer Friday’s NFP miss as lower yields increase their paper wealth (yields promptly reversed), employment within Financial Services, Information, and IT Services continues to slowly decline, with the 2026 YTD decline in Financials employment being the most significant decline in the last 10 years outside of the Wuhan Flu.

Some might quickly say “this is a natural adjustment to the COVID hiring spree” or “these organizations were already bloated”, and that is probably partially true, but there are also clearly structural changes at work.

Ask any investment banker about Rogo, or any Big Four accountant about Internal AI usage. What were previously glitchy and incompetent AI tools now operate at the level of an entry level analyst. They aren’t perfect, obviously, but they are advancing at breakneck speeds and enabling more seasoned employees to get much more done. The sheer payoff for products that work is exactly why Wall Street and VCs are willing to throw hundreds of Millions at any startup that offers an edge.

AI bears frequently cite the “looseness” of these investments and the large number of middlemen within the AI supply chain as evidence it’s one giant bubble, and they’re partially right. Oracle, Google, Microsoft and Amazon are renting out chips at a 25-40% margin, purchased from Nvidia who makes a 70% gross margin, who buys components and memory from suppliers at an astounding 80% gross margin. So many layers of middlemen at 50-80% gross margins, it makes the US Healthcare system look relatively well behaved in comparison.

While your first thought might be this is indicative of a bubble, perhaps it’s also an indication that the payoff of genuinely helpful AI far exceeds its cost, which is why people are willing to invest so much and overpay in the first place. Over the past several months, nearly every hyperscaler and neocloud has raised prices, AWS with a 15% increase this month, Coreweave with a 20% increase in July followed by a smaller increase this month, and Nebius with sizeable increases in May (and also likely this month). I’m not here to say the Frontier Lab business model works (I really don’t know and if anything I lean towards no), but from overall token usage and outsized demand for inference to run open source Chinese models, it seems clear the benefit AI provides far exceeds the cost, which is why anyone with capacity quickly sells out.

Now, the question is, aside from a direct exposure to AI names, how can we benefit from this trend investing-wise? I think the answer is simple: keep a diversified Portfolio of companies at attractive multiples returning cash to the shareholders that are insulated from AI, and simply steer clear of AI challenged names no matter how cheap they may seem.

I think my February 3rd piece on positioning for upside illustrates this well. At the time, a basket of vulnerable software-heavy BDCs were trading at “the largest discount since the financial crisis”, and IES Holdings (an electrical and infrastructure contractor that designs, fabricates, and installs power and communications systems) was trading at a steep discount to industry peers. Both seemed relatively inexpensive relative to historical multiples and invited attention. The software-heavy BDCs, however, were heavily AI vulnerable and had capped upside (who wants to pay above NAV for software loans?) while IES was at an already palatable 17x earnings multiple with sizable insider ownership and 30% growth, and had upside potential if infrastructure investment accelerated.

Since the article, IES is up 61% as earnings have boomed, while 4 out of the 5 BDCs have hit fresh lows after cutting dividends and writing off assets. There are plenty of cheap stocks, but most are cheap for a reason. With factor moves and AI risk increasingly whipsawing equities, I think selectivity is key and that it’s a stockpicker’s market.

In this Portfolio Review, I’ll be covering recent additions and removals to my Portfolio, my thoughts on the components within each of the five baskets: US Financials, Global Financials, Memory and Storage, Tech / AI Infrastructure, and Assorted Value, and the levels where I’m looking to add and reduce exposure to existing names.

Recap of Removals:

Before we get into the current Portfolio, I wanted to briefly touch on the trades discussed in the chat, and the reasoning behind each removal.

1. CBL Properties (CBL) +114% - Exited September 15, 2026

The CBL thesis has largely played out. After substantial refinancing activity, the disposition of land parcels and non-core assets, and steady repurchase activity and dividend increases, the market has become aware of CBL’s dramatic transformation and the stock has soared from a highly-distressed 4.5x FFO multiple to a reasonable 7.5x FFO multiple.

Given overall weakness in REITs, sizeable insider and significant holder selling, and the September interest rate hike increasing the burden of CBL’s large floating rate term loan, I believe CBL no longer resembles a value setup. With a roughly 4.5% dividend yield and limited repurchase activity at these levels, I think CBL essentially mirrors broader REIT exposure at best, which is something I am not interested in. It was a contentious name and the underdog thesis clearly proved itself, but at the current valuation I don’t see upside - I’m happy to cash it in and retain the proceeds for more attractive setups.

2. Heritage Insurance Holdings (HRTG) +17% - Exited July 29, 2026

Heritage was originally featured in the “30 Days to November” piece almost a year ago. At the time, it was trading just over 5x earnings, with an immediate tailwind from no summer hurricane activity and significant growth opportunities in NY and CA. Since then, the company has executed well on its expansion plans and the stock soared during the June-August “flight to safety” as value names roared back. My sale was poorly timed, just a few days after selling in July, Heritage reported blowout earnings and soared to an all time high of 35 a share.

I have a lot of respect for Heritage, they have turned the company around from a 20 cent penny stock in 2022 into a well-regarded US Insurer with significant ties to FL, CA, and NY and the broader Northeast. There are very few insurers of Heritage’s limited size that have such significant geographic diversification and experience. Nonetheless, Homeowner’s Insurance competition is rapidly intensifying in FL and the US, I think the market is not yet recognizing the risk lower insurance rates pose to 2027 and 2028 results. Heritage is likely to crush the Q3 EPS estimate of $0.77 given there were no major storms and the loss environment was benign this quarter, so perhaps it’s worth considering a short-term earnings trade, but I’d only be interested in buying back in for the long haul at a bargain valuation, which is still just $25 a share.

3. Waterstone Financial (WSBF) +42% - Exited July 29, 2026

Waterstone Financial, a highly rate-sensitive Regional Bank, was originally featured in “Shifting Into Rates Down” on August 29, 2025. At the time, the stock was trading at a 25% discount to Tangible Book Value with a sizeable repurchase program, growing earnings, and a mortgage arm highly geared towards falling interest rates.

In July, Waterstone finally crept above its own Tangible Book Value, providing a pleasant exit opportunity after trouncing the broader regional bank benchmark by 22%. With historically limited repurchase activity above Tangible Book Value, and higher interest rates impacting its Net Interest Margin and slowing underwriting opportunities for its Mortgage Arm, I think it’s time to let it go. Since July, despite the stock’s strong performance, mortgage rates have surged into the 7 - 7.50% range, which is going to severely dampen the Mortgage arm in Q4, and Real Estate activity across the country. Waterstone isn’t a name to forget, however. Chances are it becomes a strong buy once mortgage and interest rates finally begin to decline, and I’ll be keeping it on my watchlist as a “Rates Down” name for this scenario.

4. Farmer Mac (AGM and AGM/A) +30% - Exited July 27, 2026

Farmer Mac is a privately owned Government Sponsored Enterprise (GSE) that purchases and guarantees agricultural loans. At the time of position entry, AGM was trading at just 8x earnings (a historical 10 year low), amidst credit quality concerns which prompted a huge plunge in the stock. Since then positive results have soothed concerns - credit quality has stabilized, the dividend was increased, and AGM flexed its share repurchase capabilities in the $160 - $180 range. In typical fashion, the stock jumped a further 12% since the sale, but I’m happy with the exit. AGM historically trades within a stable band of 8x - 12x earnings, and closer to 8x or 9x earnings in the $180 - $190 range I will happily re-enter. Contrary to popular belief, AGM is one of the best performing financials names over the last 10 years, generating an annualized return of 21%, way ahead of peers and the S&P. I believe an attractive level to watch is $180, which represents a long-term opportunity.

5. Ategrity Specialty Insurance (ASIC) +39% - Exited September 28, 2026

Ategrity Specialty insurance was originally featured last December as a pair trade against its well-known peer, Kinsale Capital Group. Since then, Ategrity has defied industry headwinds, generating Gross Premium growth of around 25%, 20% ahead of the industry.

With the stock now trading at 15x earnings I think the valuation has gotten lofty. It’s possible Ategrity becomes the new “growth darling” as investors look for faster growing opportunities within insurance, but I also think you need to contextualize the valuation with the broader overall trend: Excess and Surplus lines growth has slowed from 15% in 2025 to just 3% YTD in 2026, a significant deceleration. At 10x earnings with 25% growth it was an easy entry, but at 15x earnings with a huge industry headwind, I just don’t feel comfortable holding it. There are plenty of other Portfolio positions at a single digit multiple with significant share repurchase activity, I’d much rather allocate to them than hold Ategrity and hope momentum continues driving it higher.

6. Entravision Communications (EVC) +171% - Exited August 21 Via Options

Entravision was trading at a 7% dividend yield with essentially zero value ascribed to its rapidly growing advertising segment, Smadex, at the time of entry in the March Portfolio review. Since then, Entravision has reported 100% YOY growth and great operating leverage, but the stock fell below the $10 August protective puts I purchased and was subsequently closed out.

(Excerpt from the August 10th earnings Note)

One of the reasons I like purchasing put protection is that it holds you accountable, and additionally, for small caps, it’s the only way to have a defined exit strategy. Stop orders are unusable for earnings since they could trigger after hours and lead to wild execution, and more importantly, a put position provides an extra line of defense against negotiating with yourself. Unlike a literal or mental stop (which you can easily adjust), a long position paired with a put sets clear time and price conditions on how much leeway you are willing to give.

Either the name you own starts behaving properly, or it’s removed and you move on at options expiration.

In this instance, after riding Entravision up from $3 a share to $13 only to see it fall precipitously from $11, I trimmed 25% of the position prior to earnings and used a portion of the profits to eliminate downside risk below $10. Despite very impressive results, Entravision’s conservative guidance for Q3 wasn’t enough to impress the market, and by mid August it was trading at $8.50, sharply below the $10 Strike Puts and was “put away”.

I will discuss in further detail below, I’ve put on a similar protective put trade on Western Digital. Despite the stock being up 120% YTD and contributing heavily to returns, it’s down 44% from its June highs, and simply isn’t performing like Micron, Samsung, and Hynix. There’s a limit to how much of a drawdown I’m willing to take, and Western Digital is nearing that pain point.

Back to Entravision, the stock has since drifted down into the low 7s, and is starting to look interesting. Will give it a closer look towards earnings, which should be reported in late October.

7. Powell Industries (POWL) +136% - Exited August 21 Via Options

My favorite way to hedge the AI Infrastructure names (FIX and IESC, formerly Powell) is via costless collars. Almost all AI Infrastructure / Electrification names exhibit positive skew going into earnings, which means you can substantially reduce downside and cap upside by purchasing puts and selling calls, usually at a small credit provided the strikes are equally distant.

AI Infrastructure basket components regularly exhibit a stairs up, elevator down pattern, which made continual collars ideal. Comfort Systems and IES Holdings were able to quickly rebound in August after a huge liquidation within the AI trade, whereas Powell wasn’t able to stay within the 250 / 300 Collar after disappointing earnings.

Normally, if collared names are somewhat close to the bottom range of a collar, I’m willing to cash the put in to keep the trade going. In this case, Powell was 30% below the $250 Put, and was also trading above 35x earnings with disappointing growth numbers, while IES traded below 25x earnings with 35% growth. I let the Powell position get put away at options expiration to add more firepower for adding IESC near $300.

8. Vistance Networks (VISN) -20% - Exited August 6

I originally pitched Vistance back when it was still known as Commscope in 2024, but because I re-pitched in May I think it’s only fair to refer to the more recent entry point.

I didn’t like the commentary on the Q3 call that Vistance is eating a chunk of higher memory prices rather than passing the entirety through to their large cable customers. Ultimately, despite Vistance’s extremely cheap valuation, I think high memory prices will be an issue for years and a large negative for the company unless it starts passing through these costs. I cut the loss at 21%.

9. Hello Group (MOMO) -21% - Exited September 10

Hello Group is a melting ice-cube, a Chinese dating app owner with a huge cash balance (almost $8 a share), a growing portfolio of International apps, and a cash-cow portfolio of domestic apps in steady decline.

Hello Group’s June results showed strong growth in their International Portfolio and upbeat sentiment which kept me interested, but their September report was a significant departure from June: International app growth slowed, and the 2027 International growth target was lowered.

With few, rare, exceptions, I exit new positions when they hit a 20% loss. Despite MOMO’s significant discount to its own cash balance and relatively compelling fundamentals, I think the overall decline in China Internet related equities (KWEB) and the prospect of tax-loss selling by individual investors towards the end of the year creates a difficult backdrop to stay invested. I took the 21% loss, and may revisit the stock early next year if International Growth gets back on track.

10. SK Square (402340) +44% - Exited October 1

SK Square was the first Korean stock I purchased on IBKR back in April. I remember sitting at my screen at 2:10 AM EST in late April the day IBKR launched Korean Equities, continually typing Korean tickers into TWS, none of them would appear as symbols. Eventually, SK Square loaded and I was able to buy.

It’s been a nauseating ride ever since. My initial 2% of NAV investment ballooned into a 150% gain, before crashing right back to cost basis in August and since recovering to +44%. I’m not turning into a Memory bear, and it’s undeniable that SK Square is the cheapest way to get exposure to Memory given it trades at a 45% discount to the value of its Hynix stake, which itself is just around 4.5x 2027 Earnings.

Still, after the events of July, there’s a limit to how much Memory and Storage risk I’m willing to take, and that’s a very firm 25% of my Portfolio. With the recovery of Hynix, Samsung Preferred, and Micron over the past couple of weeks (no thanks to WDC), I was once again above that 25%. Given the smaller gain in SK Square relative to the other basket positions, I sold SK Square. If I was approaching this from a fresh slate and had no exposure to Hynix, I would certainly consider SK Square for memory exposure.

As I’ll discuss below, of all the components within the Memory and Storage Basket (Samsung Preferred, Hynix, Western Digital, Micron, and Kioxia), Samsung Preferred is still my favorite given the sizeable discount to the Common Shares, and Samsung’s variable dividend approach, which creates a direct cash incentive to own the Preferred Shares over the Common, as opposed to a buyback which might benefit the Common with minimal impact on the Preferred.

11. Global Medical Response Solutions (GMRS) +10% - Exited July 2

Global Medical Response is America's largest privately owned ambulance and air transport company. The IPO flopped horribly, and the shares dropped from $15 to just $10.50 in weeks. After several lofty initiations of coverage (GS at $30, UBS at $20), a short-term setup presented itself, and the position was quickly closed after the initiations of coverage attracted Institutional attention.

Interestingly, the stock has entirely retraced the rally and is once again hovering around 7x earnings, but I think caution is warranted. GMR is highly levered, and has indicated it will use its earnings to pay off its sizeable debt load. Until a shareholder friendly dividend or repurchase plan is announced, I will be watching from the sidelines.

The removal of these eleven names has freed up a lot of dry powder, and my cash pile is now sitting at roughly 25%. I’d like that figure to be a bit lower, but with interest rates going haywire and midterm mayhem just beginning to kick off, I don’t mind waiting a few weeks, or even months to get that money to work. As with all of the single-name articles I’ve posted on this blog, International General Insurance, CBL Associates, Oppenheimer Holdings, Chain Bridge Bancorp, and Customers Bank, what made them work was the entry point. Rather than put all that “cash to work” immediately, I’d rather closely follow names I’m interested in, and wait for an attractive entry point to bet big.

Recap of Additions:

1. ABC Arbitrage (ABCA FP) - Added September 3

Article: “Buying the Buyback”

Forward P/E: 7.5x, Dividend Yield: 7.5%, Price Target: 6.50 Eur

ABC Arbitrage is the only publicly listed statistical arbitrage specialist, with a history of success spanning 31 consecutive profitable years since inception in 1995. As expected, H1 results were a blowout 0.43 EUR, driven by significant investment profits from ABC’s Reversion and Opportunities flagship funds.

H1 results were the strongest in a decade, and I think ABC is poised to build on its excellent results in the second half. ABC’s Reversion and Opportunities funds are up a further 14% and 6% respectively, and the company also stated it is aiming for 250 Million in external assets by 1H 2027, nearly triple the 74 Million it started 2026 with. I think ABC Arbitrage represents one of the only ways to add Hedge Fund Level Statistical Arbitrage to your portfolio (the other being Hamilton Global, HG, a US Insurer who has billions invested in a special fund run by Two Sigma), and that at 7.5x forward earnings (assuming the funds hold their performance) the stock is simply too cheap to ignore. It is important to note that ABC Arbitrage is likely seen as PFIC under US Tax Code. I will be keeping a close eye on their September performance once it is released, and am looking for near-term upside to 6.00 EUR a share. It’s a 2% position for me, and I would be very happy to add in the 5.00 - 5.50 range again, should the stock return there.

2. Semitec (6626 JT) - Added September 3

Article: “Buying the Buyback”

Forward P/E: 10x, Dividend Yield: 2.5%, Price to Tangible Book: 0.95x, Price Target: 2,600 JPY

Semitec Corp is a leading global manufacturer of high-precision temperature sensors. Unlike the commodity-like offerings of its peers, Semitec’s time-tested thin-film thermistors are primarily used in Medical Device and Battery Thermal Management applications and command superior margins.

Despite being tightly held by the founding family (who still own almost half the company), Semitec has exhibited surprisingly shareholder-friendly capital allocation, repurchasing 10% of the float this year and tripling the dividend from 2022 levels. Even amidst the larger cash outlays, Semitec has nearly 750 Yen in net cash per share, more than enough cash to continue growing the business via two planned factories, while also continuing to reward shareholders. I have several orders in the 2,200 to 2,300 Yen range, which I believe offers an attractive entry point, and am excited for their FY Q1 earnings report, which should come out in early November.

3. A Plus Asset Advisors (244920 KS) - Added September 3

Article: “Buying the Buyback”

Forward P/E: 9x, Dividend Yield: 2.5%, Price to Tangible Book: 1.7x, Price Target: 14,500 KRW

A Plus Asset Advisors is one of Korea’s only publicly listed insurance brokerages. The business is inherently capital-light, and is poised to benefit from increasing consumer preference to purchase insurance via independent agents, and regulatory crackdowns on aggressive competitors.

A Plus is currently a 1% position for me, I have an order to add another 0.25% near 12,000, a further 0.25% at 11,500, and 0.50% at 11,000. Given A Plus’s fee-based nature and consistent growth, I think the expected forward return increases materially if you are able to get it at 8x earnings, which would be just over 10,900 Won a share. The company is steadily executing its 650,000 share repurchase program, approximately 120,000 shares remain to be executed before year end (about 5% of the average daily volume). Earnings should be out in mid-November, and I expect A Plus to follow through on its commitment to publish a more detailed “Value Up” program, a Korean regulatory filing detailing 3-Year ROE, PBR, and shareholder return forecasts. A Plus is a name that will take time, but I believe the steady nature of its insurance brokerage, highly aligned insiders, and an activist Korean hedge fund, who no pun intended is named Align Partners and owns 20%, helps ensure shareholder friendly capital allocation will continue.

4. GoDaddy (GDDY) - Added September 21

Chat: September 21

Forward P/E: 12.5x, Price Target: $110

There has been a whirlwind of news surrounding GoDaddy since the initial entry on September 21st.

On September 24th, the Financial Times reported Gen Digital (GEN) had approached GoDaddy with an acquisition offer, sending shares to $110 before they reversed the following day. Unfortunately, I wasn’t at my screen when the news hit, and would’ve gladly exited at that level.

Since the 24th, I’ve increased the GoDaddy position at $95 to 1.5%, and will add another 0.5% in the low 90s. I’ve also been writing January $80 Strike puts on another 0.50% notional amount of shares.

The GoDaddy thesis is simple: GoDaddy is seen as a loser facing multiple challenges across website design and cheaper domain registrars but the data points to the opposite.

Rather than rely on anecdotal evidence (it is true Namecheap offers .com domains at $16 and Cloudflare at a razor thin $11 - they probably don’t even make money on it), I started scraping .tld (top level domain) data from ICANN, the World’s domain registrar.

The data seems to indicate GoDaddy’s new Airo AI Offering has entirely stopped atrophy in its tracks. Clients who might’ve moved to Wix (or peers) for a sharper, snapier design, are increasingly staying at GoDaddy.

For the first time since 2023, net domain transfers on a TTM basis have turned positive, clients are moving roughly 50,000 domains to GoDaddy a year as opposed to from.

Additionally, GoDaddy’s promotional activities are finally yielding results, GoDaddy’s Global Domain count is rebounding sharply from -2% on a TTM basis, and likely turned positive in Q3, the first positive reading since 2022. It’s important to note the ICANN .tld data is on a three month delay.

I’m not here to say GoDaddy is the greatest domain registrar in the World (it probably isn’t). Still, I think the mistake Wall Street is making is assuming a cheaper alternative automatically wins.

I think that, most people who own a domain simply don’t care.

A fraction of all registered domains are actually used for websites, domain names represent a future business idea, a memory, an email address, or perhaps even a dream. $22 a year to keep a dream alive isn’t that much.

The client base is stickier than it seems. Changing registrars frequently involves changing nameservers as well. The process is highly labor intensive, may lead to downtime, and can be an absolute disaster if you have email connected to one nameserver that doesn’t switch over properly. The sheer hassle to save $6 or even $9 a year isn’t worth it to most.

One of the more recent arguments against GoDaddy is that AI overviews for “cheap domain names” frequently recommend Namecheap or Cloudflare. This obviously isn’t great news, but it also isn’t a surprise, it’s been like this for years. Any traditional Google query (traditional Google query, talk about a change in the times) for “cheap domain” within the last five years has always listed Namecheap first.

I dislike GoDaddy’s management team, and think it’s embarrassing they happily collect their Stock Based Compensation while the stock itself has gone nowhere over the last decade. Based on my own framework, the management alignment score here is a zero.

With all of this in mind, I think GoDaddy is still doing alright, and that the stock is cheap enough to work. The company is finally turning on the share repurchase aggression, and bought back half a Billion in stock last quarter at $84 a share. The stock is trading at a palatable 12.5x earnings without any wild “reconciliations”, and can likely continue “milking” customers for an extra 1-2% a year.

Given the lack of management alignment, or even credibility, it’s impossible for GoDaddy to ever be a high conviction trade for me, but at the current valuation I’m willing to make it a low conviction trade. Ultimately aiming for GoDaddy to be a 2.5% position, inclusive of the put selling (counting each put as long 100 shares), not large enough to cause destruction if things really go wrong, but sizeable enough to pack a punch if the data trend proves to be true. I’m expecting a really sizeable reaction to earnings which should be released at the end of October. Short interest in the stock has jumped from 5 Million shares in August to almost 8 Million shares in September, it’s clear a lot of people really dislike GoDaddy. Guess we’ll see if they’re right.

On a side note, I know I began this piece with “steer clear of AI vulnerable names”. Mildly breaking my own rules here, but at an extremely small weight.

5. Short American Coastal (ACIC) - Added June 28

Chat: June 28

Forward P/E: 7.5x-9x, Price to Tangible Book Value: 1.53x

American Coastal is a leading underwriter of Commercial Property and Casualty insurance in Florida, with a specialty in older Catwalk Buildings.

One of the benefits of trading closely correlated insurance companies is they occasionally discuss each other’s results. What really caught my interest earlier this year was Heritage’s commentary on the Commercial Insurance market, which they described as “inadequately priced” when explaining why their Commercial revenues declined precipitously.

Unlike homeowner’s insurance, which reprices much more slowly as they are small ticket policies, Commercial Insurance for large buildings is a fiercely competitive market. If an HOA can reduce the cost of insurance from $500,000 to $450,000, it’s worth their time.

American Coastal was initially paired as a short leg against Heritage, which I closed in July. Since the short call on American Coastal, the stock has dribbled down from $11 towards a much more reasonable $9 a share.

To be clear, American Coastal is a well-run underwriter with aligned leadership, I’m not disputing that. They simply happen to be at the wrong place at the wrong time, competitors (whether adequately priced or not) are underwriting at extremely affordable rates, which makes it tough to hold market share. Even with no major storms, I expect ACIC’s EPS to decelerate significantly from $2.02 over the last twelve months, to just $1.20 in 2027, a deceleration I believe the market is not yet attentive to and could shake out several of the large growth investors who seem to not be touching their positions.

With the HRTG Long closed, however, there isn’t much of a need for short insurance exposure and I’m neutral on the name in the low 9s. As a result, I’ve reduced my short to a token position now, but have set an alert to add back exposure if it trades above $10. I’d also quickly add back exposure as a pair trade if HRTG falls into a buying range.

6. Short J.P Morgan (JPM) - Added September 28

Chat: September 28

I’ve been a Citi bull and a Jane Fraser fan for a very long time. After the multi-year run, sadly, I think the easy money is coming to an end and that the “agentic” narrative promoted by Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok may weigh on banks over the next few weeks.

The “Agentic” thesis being circulated is that consumer AI agents may one day “sweep” idle cash sitting in a 0% APY checking account at big bank to high yield savings account offered by online competitors. To be upfront, I find the thesis unlikely. Large institutions like JPM already hate giving out data to third party fintechs, and I’d imagine if an “agentic connector” started immediately wiring out Millions of dollars across thousands of client accounts, it would be banned faster than an independent journalist at the entrance of a World Economic Forum event.

Still, Torsten’s thesis has merit. While the launch of Muse drove both Regional Banks and the Big 4 (JPM, Bank of America, Wells, and Citi), down, it’s important to note that Regional Banks are much more competitive for retail deposits than the Big 4, and that the Big 4 pay extremely little for their bountiful retail deposits. For all their huff and puff about “caring about the community”, the Big 4 happily pay just 0.01%, or in the case of Chase, 0.02% if you are a “Private Client”. Wow!

I also think the higher rate environment prompts a continual impulse among depositors to finally “take the leap” and move to an online bank. Why leave thousands, or tens of thousands, in a 0.01% checking account when full service online banks like Ally offer 3% or more?

Luckily, of the Big 4, Citi has lower reliance on retail deposits as a result of its large presence in payments services, but given a general “cooling off” in banks and the recent Muse impulse, I wanted to temporarily reduce exposure rather than close out a 125% winner. I did this by shorting JPM against my Citi position.

Citi trades at a much more palatable 10.3x 2027 versus JPM’s 13.2x, and also has much more aggressive capital allocation (repurchasing 1.7% of shares last quarter versus JPM at just 0.7%), so there is a slight fundamental impulse behind this trade in addition to my desire to reduce exposure. JPM may also suffer from the “Building / Naming curse”, a commonly held belief (that I agree with) that any bank or financial institution suffers a few years of mediocre results immediately after purchasing the naming rights to a stadium, sporting event, or building a shiny new HQ.

The short has already helped out a bit, and I intend to keep it until it feels like the coast is clear within large banks.

7. Short Uber $85 January Calls (UBER) - Added September 28

Chat: September 28

I’ve noticed Uber competitor Empower is springing up across the United States. If you ask people in New York or Miami, the app is rapidly gaining market share by offering rides at 25-30% discounts to Uber. This isn’t merely speculation, I use the app myself in New York and it regularly offers long distance rides at a significant discount. The allure of the app is it passes through all earnings to the drivers and charges them a flat, monthly subscription fee. Drivers earn more, and riders pay less.

Rather than short Uber shares outright, I sold January $85 calls corresponding to the proportional number of shares I would have shorted for a 0.5% short position. To be clear, the sizing is based on the underlying share exposure not the price of the option. The calls were originally $1.41, and are now trading at $1.15.

Portfolio Holdings:

Memory and Storage (25% Gross, 20% Net after Options):

Potential Entry Levels

  • Samsung Preferred (005935 KS) < 185,000

I’ve kept the weight of the Memory and Storage basket stable at 25% of my Portfolio since the June review. I’ve steadily added to Samsung Preferred, reduced exposure to Hynix via the sale of SK Square, purchased protective puts on Western Digital on Friday, and collared Micron between 1,000 and 1,500 until January 2027 options expiration.

I’m still a Memory bull, but the setup is admittedly more difficult over the next couple of weeks. The stabilizing effect of Samsung and Hynix’s repurchase program is imminently about to end. My calculations indicate Samsung’s repurchase program will run out of capacity this Wednesday, and Hynix’s program will run out of capacity by October 20th.

The combined programs contributed $1.23 Billion USD in daily net buying from late August to the present, and the impact has been notable: there have been no market halts and Memory finally feels investable as opposed to a casino. The lack of share repurchase activity in late October is likely to exacerbate pre-earnings volatility. Additionally, Korean analysts tend to high-ball estimates to justify bullish price targets, which creates a high bar to beat in late October.

Before I get further into the Memory trade, I want to discuss some important updates within Hard Drives and Storage.

On Friday, a Nikkei report on Toshiba’s Philippines Expansion Plans sent Western Digital and Seagate down 10% each. The report was partially mis-stated by newswires: Toshiba is aiming to double FY 2025 Exabyte volume by FY 2027 (not 2x unit output). Strangely, the news came out late Thursday night to no impact, but was picked up by TrendForce the following day.

The HDD trade has commanded a huge multiple premium over Memory and Flash for three key reasons:

  • Supply Discipline by Western Digital, Seagate, and Toshiba

  • No Threat of Chinese Competition or Model Architecture Changes

  • Limited Capex Requirements

It’s important to understand both the bull case and bear case for HDDs center around Limited Capex Requirements.

Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung have nearly $285 Billion in Property, Plant, and Equipment dedicated to Memory Production, and have budgeted a further $150 Billion in expansion capex over the next twelve months alone.

HDD Manufacturers, in contrast, have extremely limited PPE. Toshiba’s figures are not publicly available, but Western Digital and Seagate have just $5 Billion in Property, Plant, and Equipment, and $2 Billion in budgeted expansion capex over the next twelve months.

Simply put, the HDD shortage is more solvable than the Memory shortage.

If Seagate, Western Digital, and Toshiba really wanted to, they could invest $5 Billion now and close the supply demand imbalance by 2029. In contrast, the Memory producers are investing hundreds of Billions but still see no path to the supply demand imbalance resolving.

To understand why HDD Makers plunged on Friday, I think it helps to look at the situation from Toshiba’s perspective. Toshiba has steadily lost market share to Western Digital and Seagate (who have superior technology, density, and reliability, Seagate moreso than Western Digital). It’s estimated that Seagate and Western Digital control roughly 45% of the HDD market each, with Toshiba in a distant third at 10%. Right now, there is a tremendous shortage of HDDs, and the supply demand gap is projected to exacerbate itself by 2028.

Seagate and Western Digital are extremely disciplined in adding capacity, because they make more by undersupplying the market.

Contracted prices for HDD TBs are steadily increasing 4-5% a quarter, and it’s rumored that Hyperscalers are already agreeing to $30+ a TB in CY 2028. As crazy as that sounds, the numbers seem believable: HDDs are trading in the spot market at $35 - $50 a TB today as enterprises rush to meet their storage needs.

Western Digital and Seagate have realized they can make more by steadily increasing production 25% a year, and letting price increases take care of the rest. This is exactly why they aren’t in a hurry to build new facilities (which take 2 years to come online anyways). The net return on significant capex and volume expansion for them is barely positive, with 45% market share each they have more to lose via slower price increases than they have to gain via higher volume.

Toshiba, on the other hand, doesn’t have this problem. They have unit share of 18%, and Exabyte volume share much closer to 10% (around 180 EB). Toshiba gains more from higher sales than they lose to slower pricing increases given minimal market share. With spot prices and 2028 Hyperscaler negotiations at $30 a TB, it’s highly profitable for Toshiba to expand volume, which is exactly why they are investing $400 Million to do so. I think Toshiba is going for “the steal”. There are two very powerful players (Western Digital and Seagate) who have an almost unofficial detente to not flood the marketplace and destroy each other. Toshiba is small enough to play both sides and gain a little market share, without risking massive retaliation as Western Digital and Seagate would just hurt themselves by attempting to stamp out Toshiba.

In the grand scheme of things, Toshiba’s target to double production to 300 - 350 EB by 2028 isn’t enough to offset the shortage and represents a roughly 45% annual increase in volume relative to WDC and STX’s 25%, but this added volume clearly has the capability to slow future price increases.

Whenever there is a potential thesis change, I want to look at a position from the lens that I don’t already own it.

Western Digital and Seagate are currently trading at 15x / 18x CY 2027 earnings, which isn’t quite a “sky high” multiple, and I think further positive EPS revisions are to come.

The bulls can correctly assert that Toshiba has a history of making “30% market share” prognostications with zero results, and that the company is also heavily reliant on external suppliers such as NHK Spring and Resonsa who might not have capacity to help Toshiba double share. Furthermore, even if Toshiba does eventually hit a 30% market share target, it essentially “joins the cartel”, and will become similarly disincentivized from further production because slower price increases will harm them more than they profit from slightly higher shipments.

The bear argument is much simpler: the HDD case rests on disciplined capex, and Toshiba’s move could be a sign that all three might lose their cool and race to the bottom. With Memory names like Micron, Hynix, and Samsung trading under 6x earnings and Kioxia closer to 4x, it’s clear perception is key. Toshiba’s production increase has zero impact on WDC and STX’s 2027 and 2028 results, but if the market decides the thesis is broken and HDDs deserve a Flash or Memory level multiple and assigns WDC a 9x multiple, there’s a lot of downside present.

There’s a limit to how much pain I am willing to take with Western Digital. Unlike other AI exposed names like Micron, Samsung Preferred, IES, and Comfort Systems who have largely shrugged off the summer liquidation and are nearing all time highs, Western Digital continues to be a drag.

I was originally waiting to add to the position near $400 - now I’m not considering that at all. I think the bull case and bear case are both extremely potent right now, and that over the next two months the market will decide whether the HDD trade is truly finished and a lower multiple is assigned, or if this was a bump in the road.

Similar to what I did for Powell and Entravision, I’m going to let the market decide. Western Digital is up 120% and has been a big contributor this year (in addition to the 750, 810, and 900 Strike calls sold which now appear virtually worthless), but I’m unwilling to ride it down much further.

With the setup feeling extremely murky, I’ve purchased December 350 Strike Puts for $19. This limits further downside to 16%, and given all the premium we’ve collected from selling WDC calls throughout the year (that seem increasingly likely to expire worthless unless the stock somehow reclaims 650 by the end of the year), I think the puts are an inexpensive way to stay in the trade while capping downside if a complete de-rate occurs. Obviously, it stings to be in this spot and I wish I had purchased protection sooner.

As for memory, I think Micron’s excellent results and commentary about Samsung’s HBM pricing indicates the supercycle is still ongoing.

Micron, Hynix, and Samsung Preferred are all inexpensive, but I have the most confidence in Samsung Preferred. I think Samsung’s history of astute capital management (they were buying back a lot of stock in 2025 - although in fairness, Micron was prohibited from doing so) and their other key divisions such as the foundry attracting big orders from Tesla (and rumored to be in discussions with Apple and Qualcomm) demonstrates the company has a bird’s eye view of the landscape. Samsung Preferred trades at sub 3x 2027 earnings, and a 28% discount to the Common Shares.

Unlike Hynix, which appears to be favoring share repurchases, Samsung is leaning towards a variable dividend approach, which creates an immediate incentive for owning the Preferred Shares over the Common. I’ve been adding steadily to my position in the 175,000 - 185,000 Won range, roughly 2.5x 2027 earnings. If Samsung follows through on the 50% of FCF return plan via dividends, I think the forward yield on Samsung Preferred is roughly 10% - 12%.

To keep my net weight within Memory and Storage below 25%, I’ve also collared Micron. It’s not that I dislike Micron - I just have much more conviction in Samsung. I’ve reduced exposure in Micron via a January 1,000 - 1,500 collar for $42. I think this is really cheap protection - it protects 92% of Micron’s current value (eliminating downside below 1,000), and if Micron is indeed above $1,500 by January, Samsung and Hynix should be doing well.

Lastly, I continue to hold Kioxia as a low conviction trade. Of Flash, HDDs, and Memory, I think Flash is the most likely to be eventually disrupted by Chinese manufacturing, which is why I hold it a low weight. Kioxia does trade at a highly palatable 4x 2027 earnings, and I like the fact they bought back nearly $5 Billion USD of stock at 16,500 Yen a share back in early August. Despite its dramatic fall from June it’s still been a major driver of returns, and I think the company has additional levers at its disposal: further share repurchases at 4x earnings, and also listing an ADR in the US which could help close the gap with Sandisk’s 7x 2027 multiple.

Overall, despite the nauseating volatility of July and August, it’s nice to see the Memory and Storage basket largely recover. The MU collar and WDC puts take substantial risk off the table for the next two to three months while leaving a lot of upside on the table. The only component I’m willing to add to is Samsung Preferred between 175,000 and 185,000 Won.

AI Infrastructure (10%):

Potential Entry Levels:

  • IES Holdings (IESC US) < $315

  • Google (GOOGL US) < $330

The AI Infrastructure basket is a relatively small group: IES Holdings (IESC), Comfort Systems (FIX) and Google (GOOGL).

Google continues to be an ultra-conviction trade for me. I think their sizeable presence in all aspects of the AI Supply Chain gives them a long-term view of where the World is moving. While many see a glass half empty scenario in Google given their underperforming models and lack of an “Agent”, I see it the other way: the stock is reasonably valued and has more to gain once Google catches up.

It’s hard for me to imagine anyone with as much reach as Google. Meta has Threads, Facebook, and Instagram, Microsoft keeps people trapped in Outlook, but Google has reach everywhere: Maps, Gmail, Search, Youtube, the side button on every Android summons Gemini.

In a few swift clicks or a popup notification they have an audience of Billions of people, if they wanted to. Google already has sufficient infrastructure for its own ambitions (and can rent it out when it is otherwise not needed at huge margins) and massive distribution potential, the only missing pieces are the models and Agents themselves.

Recent leaks indicate a major step up in Gemini 4 Argon from Gemini 3.5. I think the naysayer argument that the models might not be as “high IQ” as Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s is somewhat irrelevant. You don’t need a 160 IQ PHD to call a restaurant for you, or scan through your inbox for a missing email.

At 22x 2027 earnings, I think Google is very attractively priced. I never do sum-of-the-parts valuations, but I think segments such as Google’s TPU business are being ascribed very little value by the market relative to their stand-alone valuations. Google’s AI overviews have brought me back to search, I rarely use Claude or OpenAI for things I used to use Google for, and once they have a low-cost agent that can handle emails, phone calls, scan your camera roll, perhaps even operate your phone for you, I think it’ll become indispensable. I continue to add to the stock near $330, which is 21x 2027 earnings. Given how volatile the stock has been lately, there’s a decent chance it’s at that level later this week.

IES Holdings also continues to be a high conviction trade for me. Since the June 12th Portfolio review, IES announced its largest ever acquisition, $650 Million for Innovate’s DBM Global Structural Steel Business.

I think IES made an excellent deal. They paid 5.3x LTM Adjusted EBITDA for a growing backlog, and likely have immense cross-selling opportunities given their growing position in Communications Infrastructure and Data Center Construction. IES has a proven track record of successful integrations, revenue has surged 600% over the last decade, and highly-aligned Chairman Jeffrey Gendell (who owns $6.9 Billion and is also an extremely successful investor) has turned IES from a forgettable, struggling contractor in 2010 into one of the largest and most reliable industrial infrastructure services companies.

What also piques my interest in IES is that the company itself trades a nearly $300 Million Portfolio of other infrastructure positions (their 13-F is very interesting). The Portfolio routinely adds to EPS, and serves as a testament to IES’s investment prowess.

IES is currently 24x my 2027 EPS estimate of $14 a share. As a reminder, the stock is up huge since the pitch this February, and I think it makes sense to add to your position only at highly attractive levels. That level for me is $308 - $315 (22x earnings), roughly matching the broader market’s forward P/E.

Comfort Systems remains a low conviction trade for me. On the bull side, I think analyst estimates are very much on the low side, and that backlog will continue to amaze as Infrastructure projects pile up. On the bear side, Comfort Systems is already 29x 2027 earnings, and is vulnerable to the “shutting down data centers” narrative.

At $1,500 the stock is interesting, but at the current price I’m neutral on it.

US Financials (20%):

Potential Entry Levels

  • International General Insurance (IGIC US) < $24.25

  • Customers Bancorp (CUBI US) < $75

  • Chain Bridge Bancorp (CBNA US) < $45

  • Kaspi (KSPI US) < $90

The basket of US Financials continues to handily outperform the benchmarks, clocking in at 29% YTD relative to 0% for Insurance, 11% for Regional Banks, and -1% for the broader Financials benchmark.

With interest rates surging and credit concerns mounting, I think selectivity is key - I’m entirely avoiding upside rate exposed names, or anyone who isn’t at a defendable valuation.

Recently, I’ve been adding steadily to International General Insurance under $24.25, and Customers Bancorp under $75.

I view International General Insurance (IGIC) as an elite insurer - they regularly post combined ratios 4-6 percent below peers, have highly aligned insiders who have never sold a share (the founding family owns 34.5%), and aggressive capital management at current levels, which interests me in both a short-term trade to flip above $25, and also a longer-term addition. IGI had a rough start to the year with significant loss activity tied to the Middle East conflict, but still posted $1.00 in EPS. The situation has calmed considerably in Q3, and IGI has announced several new initiatives such as its India Office and new MGA Partnerships, which should help the company continue driving Gross Written Premium to record highs despite broader insurance headwinds.

I think IGI is likely to finish the year with $2.40 in EPS, placing it just over 10x earnings, and is within reach of $3.00 next year. The company has a clean balance sheet with no debt, a conservative investment Portfolio invested in short-term treasuries and bank deposits (that immediately gains from higher rates), and importantly, ample excess capital it frequently returns to shareholders. It’s a very simple story: it trades 2-3 turns below peers despite a tremendous track record and continually seeks out the most attractive risk-adjusted underwriting opportunities, which is why the stock has generated a 35%+ annualized return over the last 3 years, triple that of closely comparable peers.

Historically, IGI has been very active in repurchasing shares in the $23 - $25 range, and I anticipate Q4 will be no different. The stock has dropped significantly in recent weeks due to a large holder, Omani Investment Fund Ominvest, trimming their position down to 20%. Volume has spiked, and I think recent price action shows the shares are being absorbed quickly in the $24 - $25 range.

IGI fits my framework to a T: consistent capital returns, aligned management, and significant growth potential. I like anchoring my purchases near where a company historically buys back stock. In this case, that level is $24.25, which I believe offers an attractive short-term opportunity if you are looking to flip for a few percent, and also for a long-term hold if you want insurance exposure at a highly attractive multiple.

I’ve also been nibbling at Customers Bancorp (CUBI) below $75, which represents just 8x 2027 earnings, a nearly 3 turn multiple discount to closely comparable peers. Customers is relatively rate neutral, extremely well capitalized, and has a track record of top-quintile credit management. For banking, credibility is key, and I continually find it astounding that people are willing to bet on peers such as Metropolitan Commercial Bank (MCB) or Western Alliance Bank (WAL) despite a steady stream of “one off” issues that never seem to actually be one time problems. Similar to IGI, CUBI is also a high conviction trade for me: the management team has a great track record and is highly aligned ($125 Million in ownership), the bank is rapidly building a low cost deposit base comprised of commercial clients (Muse is not a threat), and I think Customers Bancorp’s AI initiatives position it as one of the only regional banks that is really looking far ahead into the future. I think $75 (8x 2027 earnings), is a great spot to add to an existing position, or a new starter position if this is your first time looking into the name.

After the recent run up, I’ve moved both Oppenheimer and Marex from the high conviction column to the medium conviction column. I trimmed half my Oppenheimer in July but I still love the company, and I haven’t touched a share of my Marex. Oppenheimer is truly unique in that it’s a fee based business with no left-tail risk like most insurers or banks, and the company is finally getting some recognition after posting record breaking results in Q1 and Q2 (Q1 results were impacted by a one-time legal payout). Marex has similarly posted record results. For those of you who are new to Marex, the company is a global prime brokerage and market maker catering to hedge fund and ETF clients with a specialty in Energy, Metals, and Leverage Swap offerings. The advent of 2x levered ETFs and elevated market volatility continues to serve as a tailwind, and despite the stock doubling since entry last year, the P/E is still a very reasonable 11x earnings. For now, sitting tight on both of these names and looking forward to earnings.

Chain Bridge Bancorp (CBNA) and OP Bancorp (OPBK) also continue to trade 8x earnings, a steep discount to peers, despite steady progress this year. Chain Bridge is barely a bank, it simply holds Billions in political deposits for PACs at 0% in exchange for providing banking services. As politics sadly gets more vicious, Chain Bridge is poised to rack up even larger profits. The stock precipitously dropped mid-September after the rate hike, which made zero sense. Every 0.25% rate hike is free money for Chain Bridge, and with the prospect of the midterm fight simply carrying on until 2028, I think the bank is likely to see above-average profitability. I think $45 (roughly 8.5x current earnings) represents an attractive entry point. OP Bancorp also continues to execute. The bank has an extremely high cost of deposits, which shields it from the Muse thesis that clients will flee to higher-payer banks. The stock is trading slightly below likely Q3 Tangible Book Value of $16.40, I’m certainly not selling here, but for an entry I like getting names at a discount - in this case that level is 0.85x - 0.90x Tangible Book Value, or $13.94 to $14.76 a share.

Finally, Kaspi has steadily drifted down from $105, incidentally right after Fintwit began to like the name again. I think Kaspi’s shareholder friendly dividend policy and unchallenged position within the Kazakh economy is highly attractive, but Private Equity insiders routinely seem to sell their stock as soon as it creeps above $105. Unlike most “value trap” situations, however, where you spend years for a long-winded thesis to play out, with Kaspi you are getting paid a huge dividend to ride along. I’m happy to collect 9% as Kaspi solidifies its position in Turkey and improves the reach of its Fintech arm, and I’m willing to add another 0.50% - 1% below $90.

Global Financials (15%):

Potential Entry Levels

  • Georgia Capital (CGEO LN) < 4,000 GBp

  • Halyk Savings Bank (HSBK LI) < $32

  • ABC Arbitrage (ABCA FP) < 5.50 EUR

  • iM Financial (139130 KS) < 18,500 KRW

The global financials basket has been a major contributor to this year’s outperformance. The basket has been working overtime to clean up the mess Western Digital and Kioxia have made - without them, I’d be nowhere near where I was in June.

While fundamentals are still attractive for the Japanese Banks and the yields continue to make their way higher, I’m increasingly attracted to the Korean Bank pick, iM Financial Group (under 5.5x earnings) which is now a medium conviction trade, and existing positions such as Halyk Savings Bank (4.7x earnings, 14% dividend yield).

The entire basket continues to trade at a discount to local and global peers, and importantly, the aggressive capital allocation continues.

OSB Group is the only odd one out - it hasn’t done well largely as a result of rising yields and broader selloffs in larger peers such as Barclays. I haven’t touched my position and I still like the stock, but at this point it is practically a yield proxy, as yields rise the stock moves lower. Over the long-run, I think the yield situation will normalize and OSB’s value will once again shine through, but until yields stabilize, the setup will continue to be murky which is why it has become a medium conviction setup.

As with US Financials, I like taking a basket approach with these International names. Most of them are astoundingly cheap, but they each come with unique risks. A Kazakh crackdown on the banking sector could slam Halyk, Russian tanks could roll into Georgia and Georgia Capital’s assets are confiscated. This single name risk is why the returns are so high, if Halyk were a highly liquid large cap with no left-tail risk, do you really think it would be trading at 4x earnings with a double digit yield? Probably not. By adding some of these names at small weight in a diversified manner, however, I think you can add “torque” to your Portfolio at extremely attractive multiples while avoiding the single name exposure risk that accompanies highly concentrated positioning.

Assorted Value (10%):

Potential Entry Levels

  • SE Holdings (9478 JP) < 500 JPY

  • Hyundai Green Food (453340 KS) < 19,000 KRW

  • Modern Dental Group (3600 HK) < 7.00 HKD

  • Semitec (6626 JP) < 2,300 JPY

Outside of Memory and Storage, AI Infrastructure, US Financials, and Global Financials, I’ve lumped all the other trades into the Assorted Value Basket. Obviously, there isn’t much relation between many of the names (Costco and Hyundai Green Food both operate food courts, but the positions have nothing to do with one another).

Within the assorted value basket, my approach is really simple. Start small, and add to the names with a repeated history of earnings beats and shareholder friendly capital allocation. Nearly every high conviction position started off as a tiny low conviction trade, and has been built into a larger position as a pattern of credibility is built.

SE Holdings and Incubations (9478 JP) a tiny Japanese publisher with a huge Securities Portfolio greater than the entire market cap is one of my favorite names within this basket. It currently trades at 500 Yen (just 0.65x Tangible Book Value), and regularly announces a fresh share repurchase program each quarter funded by interest and dividend income from its investment portfolio, and profits from its publishing business.

Like clockwork, Tangible Book Value per share increases, and 2-3% of outstanding shares are eaten away by the repurchase quarterly. With the Nikkei and global indices just a hair away from a fresh high, I think it’s likely SE’s investment portfolio has continued to do well. I think an entry near 500 (60% upside to Tangible Book) provides a rare opportunity to get equities exposure at a significant discount to NAV, paired with consistent share repurchases. Earnings should be out later in October, and I expect an additional share repurchase program to be announced. It is important to note that SE Holdings is likely seen as PFIC under US Tax Code.

I also continue to steadily add to the Hyundai Green Food position, which is now a high conviction trade for me. The company continues to repurchase 2-3 bps of the float each day, trades at 5.5x earnings and a 3% dividend yield, and also has a massive cash balance that can drive further expansion while ensuring shareholders still see cash returns. It’s one of the cheapest names in my portfolio, and I think the combination of extremely low P/E, growing dividend and buyback yield, and conservatively positioned balance sheet is rare to find in Korea. Hyundai Green Food’s business (catering, corporate and hospital meal preparation) has been profitable every year since it was spun off in 2017, and I think recent growth initiatives (such as soft food meals for the elderly) are an added tailwind for a name that is already incredibly attractive.

Modern Dental Group (3600 HK) also continues to make progress. H1 results were accompanied by a 45% dividend hike, and I expect the company to continue rolling up smaller dental labs across the globe, adding a boost to its already impressive organic growth. At roughly 10x earnings (versus 7x at entry), the stock is undoubtedly slightly more expensive, but I do believe the valuation is defendable given the company’s continuous expansion, and steady increases in the dividend. 7.00 HKD represents a 9.5x forward earnings multiple, which I believe is an attractive spot to add to the position.

Lastly, I wanted to address two underperformers within the basket, Itafos (IFOS CN), and Cash Converters (CCV AU).

Cash Converters revenues continue to improve, and earnings should follow suit in the second half of this year. H1 margins and income came in slightly lower than 2025 as a result of the company fully winding down its legacy loan products and investing heavily in lower-interest lending products with less credit risk. Still, it would be remiss not to admit the turnaround is taking longer than expected, and I also question why the company continues to pay a 10% dividend when it could be repurchasing shares or acquiring additional franchises. Because of this, I moved it to the medium conviction category, and am giving it just six more months. The valuation is highly attractive (9x for pawn shops as opposed to EZ Corp at 15x and FirstCash at 18x in the US - EZ Corp incidentally also happens to own 40% of Cash Converters), but I also don’t want to wait years for a turnaround that never materializes. As a result, I’m giving the position another six months, if February results show the story is on track I will happily hold, otherwise I will exit.

Itafos has also flipped from a big winner at +42%, to the year’s worst loser at -26%. Itafos reported a small loss last quarter, but there are some signs of improvement as Rio Tinto (the supplier of sulphuric acid) switched the pricing benchmark from Vancouver to the much more affordably priced Tampa Benchmark. Itafos is a very murky setup, as soon as the Strait of Hormuz opens and sulphuric acid prices come down, it will be operating at 3x-4x earnings, perhaps even lower given its product is sold at a 3-month rolling average of fertilizer prices. Until then, I think the stock is likely to operate near breakeven. I really like to stick to profitable companies, of the 43 names within the Portfolio all of them are profitable, and I have extremely thin patience for those that are not. It’s not that I believe you can’t make money with binary situations, practically the entirety of biotech investing involves patience with steady losers until a massive payoff is announced and people do extremely well with that, but it’s just not my favored type of investing. I’d much rather stick to low-multiple, insider owned setups that are able to return cash. If the Hormuz situation or sulphur prices show no signs of improvement by December, I plan on closing the position to harvest the tax loss to offset other realized gains.

Here’s a concise summary of the entry levels I am watching for various basket components

Conclusion

The past couple of months have been exhausting, and over the next couple of weeks I expect things to get even crazier. The Korean Memory Giants’ share repurchase programs are about to run dry right before earnings, Iran may be tempted to stir the pot prior to Midterms, and yields seem to be doing the limbo but with the wrong lyrics. As scary as all of this might seem, I think it pays to take a step back, go through your positioning, and simply adjust until you are comfortable with the level of risk.

This year’s market has been marked by countless headlines that prompt emotional decisions: the Iran war has been “ended” and “restarted” dozens of times, China’s AI models have “bypassed” memory constraints each month only for Memory to continue getting pricier, one reporter declares GPU Financing to be dead just hours before someone else receives VC funding cheaper than most margin loans. If you took all of these headlines at face value and traded off of them, you’d wind up in a padded cell. My approach remains the same as it has been: stay disciplined, hold reasonably valued companies at small weights, and constantly re-approach each position to try and understand what the other side is thinking.

While I am happy to provide the basket weights and positions, my goal is to simply get these names on to your radar. It’s entirely up to you to conduct your own due diligence, determine if you find the thesis attractive, and whether these trades are suitable for your portfolio. I really do believe that you can’t read conviction, you can only form it via your own research. As always, I will continue to post trade updates in the chat.
